I am studying the current Street Design Manual for Urban Areas in Kenya.

Very interesting findings. 

1. Kenya’s Street Design Manual says existing trees should be retained and trees should provide continuous shade. 

2. In practice, road geometry, movement, intersections, utilities and vehicle circulation are given measurable engineering requirements, while the value of an existing mature tree is largely expressed as a landscaping consideration.

3. It assumes you are designing an empty right-of-way and can establish a regular tree line.

The real Nairobi problem is often the opposite:

There is already a mature tree in the way of the proposed road geometry.

An Engineer would be perfectly right to apply the geometry and cut the trees. 

4. Trees are still treated as landscaping, rather than permanent urban infrastructure.

It says existing trees should be retained and planted 5–10m apart for continuous shade. Yet it lacks strong rules making road geometry, utilities and other infrastructure design around mature trees.

💡That may help explain Nairobi’s haphazard tree loss.

We need to move from “plant trees” to “protect the canopy.”

It has regressed into a filthy, chaotic slum where even areas that were once considered posh now resemble ugly concrete jungles. Garbage is everywhere, vibandas have taken over, drainage is virtually non-existent, our green spaces have disappeared, countless trees have been chopped down, raw sewage flows openly, and many places literally stink. 
The 527/- gang, I understand, they are simply doing what they have to do to put food on the table. What genuinely astonishes me are the few others who post these pictures as though Nairobi has been transformed. Have they forgotten what the rest of the city looks like, or have our standards fallen so low that two paved footpaths are now considered world-class?
